lede: Genome, chromosome, gene, allele, DNA. Five words for the same instructions at five different sizes, and the exam checks that you can tell them apart. Once the sizes are straight, the base-pairing rules turn one given percentage into all four.
can: Sort genome, chromosome, gene and allele by size, and define each one.
Describe DNA: a phosphate and sugar backbone, interlinking bases, a double helix.
Work out the percentage of any base from one percentage you are given.

text: Genome, chromosomes, genes, alleles and DNA

md: Your body is built and run by instructions, and every one of your cells carries the whole set. Four words name those instructions at four different sizes. Get the sizes straight and the rest of genetics follows.

md:
**Genome** — all of the genetic material of an organism. The whole set.
**Chromosome** — one long thread of DNA in the nucleus. A human body cell holds 46 of them.
**Gene** — a short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls one characteristic.
**Allele** — a different form of the same gene.

prompt: A short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls one characteristic is called a ____.
explain: A gene. The whole set of genetic material is the genome; a gene is one instruction inside it.

alt: A photograph of one person's chromosomes, spread out, stained in bands and sorted into matching pairs by size. The last pair, at the bottom right, is the only one whose two chromosomes are not the same length.
credit: Courtesy: National Human Genome Research Institute, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
caption: Real chromosomes, cut out and sorted into pairs. Count the pairs, not the chromosomes.
prompt: How many pairs can you count, and what is different about the pair at the bottom right?

md:
In the nucleus of a body cell the chromosomes sit in **functional pairs**: 23 pairs, so 46 chromosomes altogether. One of each pair came from the mother and one from the father.

Two kinds of cell break that rule. A **gamete** — a sperm cell or an ovum — carries only **one** of each pair, so 23 chromosomes. A **bacterium** has no nucleus at all, so its chromosomes are not in pairs either.

prompt: A human body cell holds its chromosomes in 23 functional pairs. How many chromosomes is that altogether?
explain: 23 pairs, two chromosomes in each pair, so 23 × 2 = 46.

alt: A length of DNA drawn as a flat ladder. Each upright is a chain of phosphate circles and sugar pentagons; each rung is a pair of bases, A opposite T and C opposite G. A small twisted version beside it shows the same molecule as a double helix.
caption: Two uprights, rungs between them, and a twist. That is the whole molecule.

md:
Unwind one chromosome far enough and you reach **DNA**. Drawn flat, it is a ladder.

The two uprights are the **backbone**, built from a **phosphate** and a **sugar (deoxyribose)**, over and over.

The rungs are the **bases**, and they interlink across the middle in only two ways: **A with T**, and **C with G**. Those are the base-pairing rules.

Let the ladder twist and you have the **double helix**.

prompt: In a DNA molecule, which base always pairs with C?
explain: G. The two pairs are A with T and C with G, and nothing else is possible.

title: Worked example: 28% of the bases in a length of DNA are A. Calculate the percentage that are C. [3]
md:
**Step 1 — use the pairing rule.** A only pairs with T, so there must be just as many T bases: **28%**. **[1]**
**Step 2 — take that pair off 100.** 28 + 28 = 56, and 100 − 56 = **44%** left for C and G together. **[1]**
**Step 3 — share what is left.** C pairs with G, so those two are equal: 44 ÷ 2 = **22%**. **[1]**

Check it: 28 + 28 + 22 + 22 = 100.

title: Show the halving
md: Only quite a few got this right in Summer 2025. Write the pair total, the subtraction and the halving on separate lines: each step can earn a mark.

prompt: In a different length of DNA, 31% of the bases are G. What percentage of the bases are A?
explain: G pairs with C, so C is 31% too. That is 62% used, leaving 38% to share between A and T: 19% each.

caption: The gene is the place. The allele is the version sitting in it.

md:
A **gene** is a place on a chromosome and the characteristic it controls. An **allele** is one of the versions that can sit in that place. Flower colour is the gene; the version for red and the version for white are two of its alleles.

The other pair worth separating: a **chromosome** is a structure in the nucleus, while **DNA** is the molecule it is made of. A chromosome is made of DNA in the way a book is made of paper.

prompt: Two pea plants carry the same gene for flower colour, but one holds the version for violet and the other the version for white. What word describes those two versions?
explain: Alleles: different forms of the same gene. They sit at the same place on a pair of chromosomes.

md:
**Higher tier.** The order of the bases is the code. Read it **three at a time**: each group of three — a **base triplet** — codes for one **amino acid**. Join the amino acids in that order and you have a protein.

So a length carrying 24 bases codes for 24 ÷ 3 = 8 amino acids.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "DNA and the Genome"
why: A second voice on the same four words, with the double helix drawn as you watch.

title: What to let pass in that video
md: It is made for another board, so it goes on to the Human Genome Project and to how a protein is actually built from the code. CCEA stops at the base triplet hypothesis: transcription, translation and the Human Genome Project are not examined here.

prompt: A length of DNA carries 24 bases on one strand, and three bases code for one amino acid. How many amino acids does it code for?
explain: 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Divide by three; multiplying by three is the slip to avoid.

md: This is usually a later question opened by a drawing of the molecule. The first mark is a name — the part the arrow points at, or the two substances in the backbone. The last mark is normally the base-percentage calculation, where the pair total, the subtraction and the halving each carry a mark. Stuck? Write A–T and C–G in the margin and count from there.
